blocks.caption: Shor's code is a concatenation: an outer phase-flip code over three blocks, and an inner bit-flip code inside each block.

blocks.title: The Knill-Laflamme condition
blocks.label: rem-l5-10-kl
blocks.md: A code with projector $P$ onto its code space can correct the error set $\{E_a\}$ if and only if $PE_a^\dagger E_bP = c_{ab}P$ for some numbers $c_{ab}$ forming a Hermitian matrix [@nielsenchuang]. The condition says that errors never map different code words to overlapping or differently scaled images, so no error reveals logical information. The next cell checks it numerically.

blocks.explain: The Knill-Laflamme condition holds for the bit-flip code with $\{I, X_1, X_2, X_3\}$ and fails once $Z_1$ is added; it holds for Shor's code with all 28 single-qubit Pauli errors (the identity and $X$, $Y$, $Z$ on each of nine qubits).
blocks.source:
# Knill-Laflamme check: P E_a^dagger E_b P must be a multiple of P for every pair of errors.
code = np.zeros((8, 2), dtype=complex)
code[0, 0] = code[7, 1] = 1                                # columns |000> and |111>
P = code @ code.conj().T

def knill_laflamme(errors):
    for Ea in errors:
        for Eb in errors:
            M = P @ Ea.conj().T @ Eb @ P
            if not np.allclose(M, (np.trace(M) / 2) * P):
                return False
    return True

flips = [np.eye(8), op(X, 0), op(X, 1), op(X, 2)]
print('bit-flip code, errors {I, X1, X2, X3}:', knill_laflamme(flips))
print('bit-flip code, add Z1:               ', knill_laflamme(flips + [op(Z, 0)]))

# Shor's nine-qubit code against every single-qubit Pauli error (1 + 27 errors), using vectors only.
def on(v, M, j, n=9):
    t = np.moveaxis(np.tensordot(M, v.reshape([2] * n), axes=([1], [j])), 0, j)
    return t.reshape(-1)

g, h = np.eye(8)[0], np.eye(8)[7]
blk_p, blk_m = (g + h) / np.sqrt(2), (g - h) / np.sqrt(2)
L0 = np.kron(np.kron(blk_p, blk_p), blk_p)
L1 = np.kron(np.kron(blk_m, blk_m), blk_m)
errs = [None] + [(M, j) for j in range(9) for M in (X, sci.Y, Z)]
images = [(L0, L1) if e is None else (on(L0, *e), on(L1, *e)) for e in errs]
ok = all(abs(np.vdot(u[0], v[1])) < 1e-12 and abs(np.vdot(u[1], v[0])) < 1e-12
         and abs(np.vdot(u[0], v[0]) - np.vdot(u[1], v[1])) < 1e-12 for u in images for v in images)
print('Shor code, all 28 single-qubit Pauli errors:', ok)

blocks.title: Correction is not yet fault tolerance
blocks.md: Everything here assumes that encoding, syndrome measurement and recovery are perfect and that errors strike qubits independently. Real syndrome circuits are noisy and can spread one fault to several qubits. Fault-tolerant constructions handle that, and they work only when physical error rates are below a threshold that depends on the noise model and the code [@nielsenchuang; @preskill]. Current devices operate with noise of this kind and without full fault tolerance [@nisq], so a logical error rate should always be reported together with the complete procedure and the noise model.

worked_example.title: Logical error rate at p = 0.1
worked_example.problem: Each of the three qubits of the bit-flip code flips independently with probability $p = 0.1$; syndrome measurement and recovery are perfect. Find the probability of each number of flips, the logical error rate, and the improvement factor over an unencoded qubit. Repeat the last two for $p = 0.01$.
steps: Zero or one flip is corrected; two or three flips end in a logical $X$. So $p_L = 0.027 + 0.001 = 0.028$, matching $3p^2 - 2p^3 = 0.03 - 0.002$.
Improvement: $p/p_L = 0.1/0.028 \approx 3.6$. The break-even check $p(1-p)(1-2p) = 0.1 \cdot 0.9 \cdot 0.8 = 0.072 = p - p_L$ is positive.
worked_example.result: $p_L = 0.028$ at $p = 0.1$ and $0.000298$ at $p = 0.01$: because $p_L \approx 3p^2$, the benefit grows as the physical error rate falls, under this noise model only.

exercises.prompt: Apply $\mathcal{D}_{0.4}$ to $|1\rangle\langle 1|$. Give the output matrix, the $Z$-basis probabilities, and the purity.
exercises.solution: $0.6\operatorname{diag}(0, 1) + 0.4\operatorname{diag}(\tfrac12, \tfrac12) = \operatorname{diag}(0.2, 0.8)$. The probabilities are 0.2 for outcome 0 and 0.8 for outcome 1, and the purity is $0.04 + 0.64 = 0.68$. The Bloch vector shrank from $(0, 0, -1)$ to $(0, 0, -0.6)$.

exercises.prompt: An $X$ hits qubit 3 of $\alpha|000\rangle + \beta|111\rangle$. Write the state, the values of $Z_1Z_2$ and $Z_2Z_3$, and the recovery.
exercises.solution: The state is $\alpha|001\rangle + \beta|110\rangle$. Qubits 1 and 2 agree, so $Z_1Z_2 = +1$; qubits 2 and 3 disagree, so $Z_2Z_3 = -1$. The syndrome points to qubit 3, and applying $X_3$ restores $\alpha|000\rangle + \beta|111\rangle$.

exercises.prompt: Flips hit qubits 1 and 2. Follow the syndrome and the recovery and say what logical operation results.
exercises.solution: The state is $\alpha|110\rangle + \beta|001\rangle$. $Z_1Z_2 = +1$ and $Z_2Z_3 = -1$, the syndrome of $X_3$. The recovery applies $X_3$, giving $\alpha|111\rangle + \beta|000\rangle = X_L(\alpha|0_L\rangle + \beta|1_L\rangle)$: a logical bit flip, which is why two flips count as a failure in [](#eq-l5-10-pl).

exercises.prompt: Show that $\mathcal{Z}_q$ leaves all $Z$-basis probabilities unchanged. The state $|{+}\rangle$ is sent through an unknown phase-flip channel and $\langle X\rangle$ is measured to be 0.8. Find $q$.
exercises.solution: By [](#prop-l5-10-bloch), $r_z$ is unchanged, and the $Z$-basis probabilities are $(1 \pm r_z)/2$. For $|{+}\rangle$, $r_x = 1$ becomes $1 - 2q = 0.8$, so $q = 0.1$.

exercises.prompt: Show that under independent bit flips with probability $p$ and perfect correction, the encoded qubit undergoes exactly the bit-flip channel $\rho_L \mapsto (1 - p_L)\rho_L + p_L X_L\rho_L X_L$ with $p_L = 3p^2 - 2p^3$, where $X_L = X_1X_2X_3$.
exercises.solution: Each flip pattern $F \subseteq \{1, 2, 3\}$ occurs with probability $p^{|F|}(1 - p)^{3 - |F|}$ and applies $X_F = \prod_{j \in F}X_j$. For $|F| \le 1$ the syndrome identifies $F$ and recovery gives $I$. For $|F| = 2$ the syndrome is that of the missing qubit $k$, and recovery gives $X_kX_F = X_1X_2X_3 = X_L$. For $|F| = 3$ the syndrome is trivial and the net operation is $X_L$. Because every outcome ends in either $I$ or $X_L$ on the code space, the overall map is $(1 - p_L)\rho_L + p_L X_L\rho_L X_L$ with $p_L = 3p^2(1 - p) + p^3 = 3p^2 - 2p^3$.

exercises.prompt: In Shor's code, show that $Z_1$ and $Z_2$ have the same effect on every code state, so the code can fix a phase flip in block 1 without learning which of its qubits suffered it.
exercises.solution: $Z_1Z_2$ acts as the identity on $|000\rangle$ and on $|111\rangle$, hence on block 1 of every code word. So $Z_1|\psi_L\rangle = Z_1(Z_1Z_2)|\psi_L\rangle = Z_2|\psi_L\rangle$, using $Z_1^2 = I$. Applying $Z_1$ as the recovery undoes a $Z_2$ error as well: $Z_1Z_2|\psi_L\rangle = |\psi_L\rangle$. Codes with this property are called degenerate.

check.question: What does a syndrome measurement seek to reveal?
options: The values of $\alpha$ and $\beta$ to within shot noise
Information about an error without reading the logical data
Independent copies of the logical state
check.explanation: The checks $Z_1Z_2$ and $Z_2Z_3$ take definite values on every corrupted code state, so their outcomes identify a correctable error and carry no information about $\alpha$ and $\beta$. Reading the logical state would destroy it.

check.question: Each qubit of the bit-flip code flips independently with probability $p = 0.1$, and correction is perfect. What is the logical error rate?
check.explanation: Failures need at least two flips: $3p^2(1-p) + p^3 = 0.027 + 0.001 = 0.028 = 3p^2 - 2p^3$.

check.question: Which single-qubit error does the three-qubit bit-flip code fail to detect?
check.explanation: $Z_2$ commutes with both checks $Z_1Z_2$ and $Z_2Z_3$, so the syndrome stays $(+1, +1)$, and it maps $\alpha|000\rangle + \beta|111\rangle$ to $\alpha|000\rangle - \beta|111\rangle$, a logical phase flip.

check.question: Is $\rho \mapsto (1 - q)\rho + qX\rho X$ with Kraus operators $\sqrt{1 - q}\,I$ and $\sqrt q\,X$ trace preserving?
options: Yes, because $(1 - q)I + qX^\dagger X = I$
check.explanation: A Kraus map is trace preserving when $\sum_k K_k^\dagger K_k = I$. Here $(1 - q)I + qX^\dagger X = (1 - q)I + qI = I$ for every $q$.

misconceptions.claim: Encoding $\alpha|0\rangle + \beta|1\rangle$ as $\alpha|000\rangle + \beta|111\rangle$ makes three copies of the state.
misconceptions.correction: Three copies would be $(\alpha|0\rangle + \beta|1\rangle)^{\otimes 3}$, with eight terms. The code state is entangled and has two; no qubit alone holds the state, and the no-cloning property is respected.

misconceptions.claim: To correct an error you have to measure the qubits and find out what state they are in.
misconceptions.correction: The code measures only parities, which have definite values on every corrupted code state. Measuring a single data qubit in the $Z$ basis would destroy the superposition.

misconceptions.claim: Quantum errors are continuous, so no finite code can correct them.
misconceptions.correction: The syndrome measurement projects a continuous error onto one of finitely many discrete errors ([](#thm-l5-10-discrete)); correcting $I$, $X$, $Z$ and $XZ$ on each qubit corrects every single-qubit error.

misconceptions.claim: Adding more qubits to a code always lowers the error rate.
misconceptions.correction: The three-qubit code helps only for $p < 1/2$ even in the ideal model, and with noisy syndrome circuits more qubits mean more places for faults. Gains require error rates below a threshold and a fault-tolerant design.

lessons.connect: The recovery is a channel that depends on a measurement record, an instrument in the sense of [L5-07](#lesson-l5-07). Level 6 treats channels such as these as causal mechanisms between laboratories and represents them by Choi matrices. Noise models of this kind also govern what near-term variational algorithms can achieve without error correction [@nisq].
lessons.caution: Conventions: $\mathcal{D}_p(\rho) = (1 - p)\rho + pI/2$ uses a mixing weight, which equals applying each Pauli $X$, $Y$, $Z$ with probability $p/4$; the bit-flip and phase-flip channels use a flip probability $q$; the course helper `qcai.science.dephasing_kraus(p)` shrinks $r_x, r_y$ by $1 - p$, which is the phase flip with $q = p/2$. Qubits are ordered $1, 2, 3$ from the left of each ket. The formula $p_L = 3p^2 - 2p^3$ holds only for independent bit flips with perfect encoding, syndrome measurement and recovery; it is not a fault-tolerant analysis, and this lesson makes no claim about thresholds or about any device. The Monte Carlo and statevector results are classical simulations, not experiments.

instructor.why: Error correction is where the abstract rules of channels, measurement and entanglement pay off. Students see a measurement that helps rather than harms, a reason to care about which basis noise acts in, and the first honest resource accounting: three or nine physical qubits for one logical qubit, worthwhile only below a break-even error rate [@nielsenchuang; @preskill; @shor1995].
teaching_notes: Start with the classical repetition code and ask students which steps break for qubits; list cloning, measurement and continuous errors on the board and cross each off as the lesson resolves it.
Have students fill in the syndrome table themselves before showing the animation; the key observation is that both terms of every row have the same parities.
Use the interactive to locate the crossing at $p = 1/2$ and then ask why real devices would need far smaller $p$ (noisy syndromes, other error types) [@nisq].
instructor.assessment: The two stretch exercises test whether students can follow a syndrome through recovery, including a failure case. The first challenge exercise checks that they can turn the counting argument into a statement about channels.
instructor.extend: Work through the five-qubit perfect code, or show that the three-qubit code under the depolarizing channel $\mathcal{D}_p$ on each qubit still has logical error of order $p$ because of phase errors. Shor's original paper is short and readable [@shor1995], and Nielsen and Chuang, Chapter 10, continues to stabilizer codes [@nielsenchuang].

further.note: Chapter 10 covers the bit-flip, phase-flip and Shor codes, the Knill-Laflamme conditions and fault tolerance.
The original nine-qubit code.
Lecture notes, chapter 7, on quantum error correction.

unit.big_question: What can be known about a quantum system from the outcomes of measurements on it, and which operations, correlations and kinds of noise does quantum theory allow?
unit.summary: Learners write qubit states in Dirac notation, turn amplitudes into probabilities with the Born rule, and picture states and gates on the Bloch sphere. They see relative phase become counts in an interferometer, build joint systems with tensor products and tell entanglement from classical correlation. Density operators, partial traces, Kraus operators and instruments then describe mixed states, noise and measurement in full generality. The unit closes with the CHSH test and its assumptions, entropy and state tomography, and a first quantum error-correcting code, separating a noise channel from the procedure that undoes it.
unit.for_whom: Advanced undergraduates, or beginning graduate students from other fields, who are comfortable with complex numbers, linear algebra over the complex numbers, basic probability and some Python, at the level of Levels 3 and 4 of this course. No previous course in quantum mechanics is assumed.
unit.prerequisites: Complex numbers, inner products, matrices, tensor products and eigenvectors (Level 3), probability, expectation and estimation (Level 3), and the causal vocabulary of Level 4 for the Bell lesson.

time.pace: About two lessons a week for six weeks, including the project. Each lesson splits into two sittings: intuition, animations and definitions first; proofs, code and exercises second.

session_flow: Retrieve: answer the review check from an earlier lesson without notes.
See it: watch the animations and explore the interactive figure before reading the formal statements.
Prove it: read the definitions and theorems, and reconstruct one proof on paper.
Compute it: run and modify the code block, and confirm the numbers quoted in the text.
Practice: work the worked example, then at least one core, one stretch and one challenge exercise.
Reflect: answer the check questions and write two sentences on the lesson's caution and scope.

outcomes.text: Compute Born-rule probabilities for pure states in any stated orthonormal basis, place states on the Bloch sphere, and prove that global phases are unobservable.
Translate a circuit into a matrix product in the correct order, describe single-qubit gates as Bloch rotations, and predict interference after a relative phase change.
Build joint states with tensor products and decide whether a pure two-qubit state is entangled.
Work with density operators: purity, the Bloch ball, and reduced states from a partial trace.
Check that a map is a quantum channel from its Kraus operators, and separate outcome probabilities from post-measurement states with instruments.
Calculate a CHSH value, state the assumptions behind the classical bound, and account for statistical error in a claimed violation.
Reconstruct a qubit state from repeated measurements in several bases measure how mixed a state is with von Neumann entropy, and state the estimation error from finite shots.
Distinguish a noise channel from an error-correction procedure and compute when a simple code helps.

unit.evidence: Each lesson ends with three or four check questions, one of which reviews an earlier lesson, and graded exercises at core, stretch and challenge levels with full solutions. The project is a reproducible notebook and a short report, judged with a four-part rubric that rewards correct derivations, honest error bars and clearly stated assumptions.
materials: Python 3 with numpy, scipy, matplotlib and plotly (the course package qcai provides the quantum helpers)
A browser for the interactive figures and the course notebooks (Colab or Binder work)
Paper for derivations; a computer algebra system is optional
Optional: free access to a cloud quantum computer to compare simulations with hardware counts

project.title: Characterizing a noisy qubit in simulation
project.summary: Over three sessions, the learner plays experimentalist and theorist for a simulated device: prepares states, measures them with a finite number of shots, estimates a noise parameter from interference and tomography data, and decides, with error bars, whether a Bell test or an error-correcting code succeeds at that noise level.
questions: A dephasing channel of unknown strength acts between the two Hadamards of an interferometer. How well can its strength be estimated from fringe visibility with 1000 shots per phase setting?
A two-qubit Werner state has visibility v. For which v does the CHSH value exceed 2, and how many shots are needed before the violation is larger than three standard errors?
Under independent bit flips with probability p, where is the break-even point at which the three-qubit repetition code starts to beat an unencoded qubit?
steps: State the model precisely: states, gates, channel and measurement, with every convention written down.
Derive the ideal prediction on paper (fringe, CHSH value, or logical error rate) as a function of the noise parameter.
Write a seeded simulation that draws finite-shot counts from the Born rule, and check it against the derivation.
Estimate the noise parameter or the test statistic from the simulated counts, with a standard error.
Repeat across noise levels and plot estimate against truth with error bars.
Write a two-page report: claim, model, assumptions, results with uncertainty, and what a hardware run would add.

rubric.start: I described the experiment in words.
rubric.got: I wrote the states, gates, channel and measurement with their conventions.
rubric.explain: I can say which conclusions would change under a different convention and which would not.

rubric.got: I derived the prediction and checked special cases.
rubric.explain: I can prove the result and state the assumptions it needs.

rubric.got: My seeded simulation matches the derivation within the expected error.
rubric.explain: I can justify the number of shots from a standard-error calculation.

rubric.got: I reported estimates with error bars and listed the assumptions.
rubric.explain: I can explain why a simulation is not an experiment and what loopholes or noise sources a real device adds.

udl: Every animation has a full text description, and every interactive figure has a written summary of what it shows.
Each idea appears as a picture, a formula, a proof and runnable code, so learners can enter through the form that suits them.
Exercises are tiered (core, stretch, challenge); the project questions can be chosen to match interest and background.
Learners may show mastery through derivations, annotated code, short recorded explanations, or written reports.

readings.note: Chapters 1, 2, 4, 8, 10 and 11 are the main reference for the whole unit.
Lecture notes with a physicist's view of measurement, decoherence, entanglement and error correction.
Rigorous treatment of states, channels, measurements and the Choi representation, used again in Level 6.
A free course that builds the same notation with runnable examples on simulators and hardware.
Volume III motivates amplitudes and interference from two-path experiments.
The original proposal of the CHSH inequality used in L5-08.
Context on what present-day noisy devices can and cannot do.

unit.approach: The unit is planned backward from its outcomes [@ubd_whitepaper]. Each lesson moves from a puzzle and a moving picture to formal definitions, theorems with proofs, computation and graded practice [@merrill2002], with a review question in every lesson to space retrieval [@dunlosky2013]. The animations are made with Manim Community Edition [@manim_ce] from the same numbers as the text, and every page offers several ways in, following Universal Design for Learning [@udl]. The mathematics follows Nielsen and Chuang and Watrous [@nielsenchuang; @watrous], with physical motivation from Preskill and Feynman [@preskill; @feynman] and hands-on examples in the style of IBM's course [@ibm]. Claims about devices are kept modest and tied to the noisy hardware that exists today [@nisq].
